analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to sign away their right to sue in court or join class actions.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced July 30, 2026 with 8 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support, was referred to two House committees and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would void forced arbitration clauses that make workers give up their right to go to court, and would end the practice of making workers sign away their right to join class or group actions as a condition of getting a job. Workers could still choose arbitration after a dispute happens, but only with a 45-day waiting period, plain-language notice of their rights, and written consent. It would also make retaliation against a worker who refuses to arbitrate illegal, and it covers independent contractors and domestic workers, no matter how an employer labels them.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by forced arbitration clauses — estimated to include most nonunion private-sector employees — gain the right to take wage, discrimination, and other job disputes to court and to join class or collective actions, which is often the only affordable way to pursue small individual claims. Independent contractors and domestic workers are explicitly covered, and workers who refuse to sign arbitration agreements gain protection from retaliation, with a right to sue employers who retaliate and recover attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nonunion workers in forced arbitration, including contractors

how_it_helps.text: Voids any pre-dispute arbitration agreement requiring arbitration of a work dispute, so workers can no longer be forced to give up court access as a condition of employment [S2].

Voids pre-dispute waivers of joint, class, or collective claims, restoring workers' ability to band together — the bill's findings state group actions are often the only affordable way for workers to get relief for small individual harms [S2].

Allows post-dispute arbitration only if it is genuinely voluntary: not required as a condition of work, explained in plain language, signed only after a 45-day waiting period with written consent, with the legal clock paused during that wait [S2].
Prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who refuse to arbitrate, and gives workers a private right to sue over retaliation with attorney's fees [S2].

Amends the National Labor Relations Act to make it an unfair labor practice for an employer to impose or enforce agreements barring joint, class, or collective claims — overturning the Supreme Court's 2018 Epic Systems decision as a matter of statute [S2].
Covers independent contractors regardless of how they are labeled and extends to domestic workers in private households, groups often excluded from workplace protections [S2].
Puts courts, not arbitrators, in charge of deciding whether the law applies to an agreement, closing a common loophole where arbitrators rule on their own powers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use forced arbitration clauses bear the cost: they lose the ability to channel disputes into private arbitration, cap exposure, and block class actions, and would face more litigation, including group actions over wage and discrimination claims. Arbitration providers lose the volume of cases these clauses generate, and employers that retaliate against workers who refuse to arbitrate could be sued.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that use forced arbitration clauses

drawbacks.text: Banning pre-dispute arbitration removes an option that at least some individual workers find faster and cheaper than court, which can take years; the bill itself acknowledges arbitration was originally designed for disputes between businesses of similar bargaining power, but that framing means all employment disputes are pushed toward the court system [S2].

The bill applies to disputes that arise after enactment even where the arbitration clause was signed earlier, so employers and workers operating under existing agreements see those terms change without a fresh negotiation [S2].

Employers would face higher litigation and defense costs, including class actions, and some of that cost could show up in hiring or pay decisions — the tradeoff an honest supporter accepts in exchange for enforceable worker rights [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: forced individual arbitration is widely understood to suppress small wage and discrimination claims because individual cases are rarely worth pursuing, so restoring group actions changes what rights are worth on paper versus in practice. The costs fall mostly on the employers that wrote these clauses, though some disputes will be slower and costlier to resolve in court, and the near-retroactive application to existing agreements creates a one-time adjustment. On balance the design is careful — it keeps voluntary arbitration available with safeguards rather than banning arbitration outright — and the safeguards (45-day wait, plain-language notice, written consent) are aimed directly at the consent problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees in July 2026, and neither committee has taken it up with under six months left in the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the Restoring Justice for Workers Act in the House on July 30, 2026, joined by six Democratic colleagues including Rep. Robert Scott of Virginia [S1][S2][S3].
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee, the standard first step, and no markup, hearing, or floor action has followed [S4].
All eight sponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill has only 7 cosponsors total [S3].
The current Congress ends January 3, 2027, so the bill has a narrow window to clear committee and reach the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers that use forced arbitration clauses: with no committee action, the existing rules — under which most workers must arbitrate individually and cannot join class actions — stay in place, while the bill would expire at the end of the Congress unless acted on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping forced arbitration in place

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled six cosponsors

for.name: Reps. Robert Scott (VA), Suzanne Bonamici, Eleanor Holmes Norton, Hank Johnson (GA), Julia Brownley, and Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Judiciary and Education and Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and have scheduled no markup or hearing, leaving it without a path to the floor

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not prioritized the bill or scheduled floor time; no Republican members have cosponsored it

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; no votes have occurred yet, but the sponsorship pattern matches the party split that has defined arbitration-reform bills for years.

industries.industry: Employers that require arbitration (retail, hospitality, staffing, large service employers)
industries.note: These employers lose the contractual tool that moves disputes out of court and blocks class actions, which is how most workplace claims get resolved on quiet individual terms. Workers gain the practical ability to enforce wage and discrimination rights.

industries.industry: Gig economy platforms and companies using independent contractors
industries.note: The bill covers workers engaged as independent contractors regardless of the label the company uses, so platforms could no longer route contractor disputes into individual arbitration and class waivers.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers (JAMS, AAA and similar services)
industries.note: The industry's employment caseload comes largely from pre-dispute clauses this bill would void; only voluntary post-dispute arbitration would remain, a much smaller stream of business.

Union-negotiated arbitration in collective bargaining agreements is expressly preserved, and the bill strengthens the NLRA's protection of concerted legal action — consistent with what unions have long sought.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to become law this Congress. A bill introduced in late July of a two-year Congress with 8 sponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action typically dies at adjournment on January 3, 2027. The realistic paths — a committee markup or attachment to a larger moving vehicle — would require leadership to elevate it, which nothing in the record suggests has happened.
